claim: Increasing extracellular [Ca2+] ([Ca2+]o) strongly decreases intrinsic excitability in neurons.
source: Increasing extracellular [Ca2+] ([Ca2+]o) strongly decreases intrinsic excitability in neurons but the mechanism is unclear.
evidence: This is stated in the abstract as an established phenomenon, drawing on general scientific knowledge in the field.

claim: By one hypothesis, [Ca2+]o screens surface charge, reducing voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) activation.
source: By one hypothesis, [Ca2+]o screens surface charge, reducing voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) activation and by another [Ca2+]o activates Calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) closing the sodium-leak channel (NALCN).
evidence: This represents a hypothesis from the literature being tested in the study.

claim: By another hypothesis, [Ca2+]o activates Calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) closing the sodium-leak channel (NALCN).
source: By one hypothesis, [Ca2+]o screens surface charge, reducing voltage-gated sodium channel (VGSC) activation and by another [Ca2+]o activates Calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR) closing the sodium-leak channel (NALCN).
evidence: This represents an alternative hypothesis from the literature being tested in the study.

claim: Neocortical neurons from CaSR-deficient (Casr-/-) mice had more negative resting potentials than wild-type neurons.
source: Here we report that neocortical neurons from CaSR-deficient (Casr-/-) mice had more negative resting potentials and did not fire spontaneously in reduced divalent-containing solution (T0.2) in contrast with wild-type (WT).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1E.

claim: Neocortical neurons from CaSR-deficient (Casr-/-) mice did not fire spontaneously in reduced divalent-containing solution (T0.2) in contrast with wild-type (WT).
source: Here we report that neocortical neurons from CaSR-deficient (Casr-/-) mice had more negative resting potentials and did not fire spontaneously in reduced divalent-containing solution (T0.2) in contrast with wild-type (WT).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 1B.

claim: After setting membrane potential to −70 mV, T0.2 application similarly depolarized and increased action potential firing in Casr-/- and WT neurons.
source: However, after setting membrane potential to −70 mV, T0.2 application similarly depolarized and increased action potential firing in Casr-/- and WT neurons.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 2.

claim: Enhanced activation of VGSCs was the dominant contributor to the depolarization and increase in excitability by T0.2.
source: Enhanced activation of VGSCs was the dominant contributor to the depolarization and increase in excitability by T0.2 and occurred due to hyperpolarizing shifts in VGSC window currents.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study supported by experimental data in Figures 3, 5, and 6.

claim: Enhanced activation of VGSCs occurred due to hyperpolarizing shifts in VGSC window currents.
source: Enhanced activation of VGSCs was the dominant contributor to the depolarization and increase in excitability by T0.2 and occurred due to hyperpolarizing shifts in VGSC window currents.
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: CaSR deletion depolarized VGSC window currents.
source: CaSR deletion depolarized VGSC window currents but did not affect NALCN activation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figure 3.

claim: CaSR deletion did not affect NALCN activation.
source: CaSR deletion depolarized VGSC window currents but did not affect NALCN activation.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the abstract and supported by data in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: Regulation of VGSC gating by external divalents is the key mechanism mediating divalent-dependent changes in neocortical neuron excitability.
source: Regulation of VGSC gating by external divalents is the key mechanism mediating divalent-dependent changes in neocortical neuron excitability.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Movement of extracellular Ca2+, through voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (VACC), to the intracellular space is central to many processes in excitable tissues.
source: Movement of extracellular Ca2+, through voltage-activated Ca2+ channels (VACC), to the intracellular space is central to many of these processes (Ma et al., 2012a; Nanou and Catterall, 2018).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: A distinct, extracellular mechanism that is independent of synaptic transmission contributes to [Ca2+]o-dependent regulation of nerve and muscle function.
source: However, a distinct, extracellular mechanism that is independent of synaptic transmission also contributes to [Ca2+]o-dependent regulation of nerve and muscle function (Adrian and Gelfan, 1933; Weidmann, 1955; Frankenhaeuser, 1957; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic literature.

claim: Decreases in [Ca2+]o and [Mg2+]o substantially facilitate spontaneous and evoked action potential generation which represents increased intrinsic excitability.
source: Decreases in [Ca2+]o and [Mg2+]o substantially facilitate spontaneous and evoked action potential generation which represents increased intrinsic excitability (Weidmann, 1955; Frankenhaeuser, 1957; Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1957).
evidence: This is supported by citations to classic literature.

claim: Physiological neuronal activity decreases [Ca2+]o.
source: In the brain, physiological neuronal activity decreases [Ca2+]o (Nicholson et al., 1978) leading to further increases in action potential firing in neighboring neurons (Anderson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Decreases in [Ca2+]o lead to further increases in action potential firing in neighboring neurons.
source: In the brain, physiological neuronal activity decreases [Ca2+]o (Nicholson et al., 1978) leading to further increases in action potential firing in neighboring neurons (Anderson et al., 2013).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The firing patterns and computational properties of local circuits are impacted substantially by [Ca2+]o-dependent positive feedback leading to changes in brain behaviors.
source: The firing patterns and computational properties of local circuits are impacted substantially by this positive feedback leading to changes in brain behaviors (Titley et al., 2019).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Under pathological conditions, larger decreases in [Ca2+]o occur, resulting in even greater changes in circuit activity.
source: Furthermore, under pathological conditions, larger decreases in [Ca2+]o occur, resulting in even greater changes in circuit activity, and implicating [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability in the pathogenesis of brain injury (Ayata and Lauritzen, 2015).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: Reduced [Ca2+]o was proposed to shift the effective voltage-dependent gating of the sodium conductance in the hyperpolarizing direction by reducing the screening of local negative charges on the extracellular face of the membrane or channel by external Ca2+.
source: Reduced [Ca2+]o was proposed to shift the effective voltage-dependent gating of the sodium conductance in the hyperpolarizing direction by reducing the screening of local negative charges on the extracellular face of the membrane or channel by external Ca2+ (Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1957; Hille, 1968).
evidence: This is a classical hypothesis from the literature being discussed.

claim: The surface potential screening model accounted for [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability in nerves and muscle without a need for additional molecular players and was widely accepted.
source: This surface potential screening model accounted for [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability in nerves and muscle without a need for additional molecular players and was widely accepted (Hille, 2001), although direct binding of Ca2+ to the VGSC was also proposed as contributing (Armstrong and Cota, 1991).
evidence: This is a historical statement about the acceptance of a model, supported by citations.

claim: Direct binding of Ca2+ to the VGSC was also proposed as contributing to [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability.
source: This surface potential screening model accounted for [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability in nerves and muscle without a need for additional molecular players and was widely accepted (Hille, 2001), although direct binding of Ca2+ to the VGSC was also proposed as contributing (Armstrong and Cota, 1991).
evidence: This is an alternative hypothesis from the literature, supported by a citation.

claim: Activation of the sodium leak channel (NALCN) by the intracellular proteins, UNC79 and UNC80, was necessary for [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability to occur in hippocampal neurons.
source: However, this theory was challenged by new data demonstrating that activation of the sodium leak channel (NALCN), a non-selective cation channel, by the intracellular proteins, UNC79 and UNC80 (Lu et al., 2009; Lu et al., 2010) was necessary for [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability to occur in hippocampal neurons.
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature being discussed, supported by citations.

claim: Following the deletion of NALCN or UNC79, [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability was completely lost in hippocampal neurons.
source: Following the deletion of NALCN or UNC79, [Ca2+]o-dependent excitability was completely lost suggesting the increased excitability resulted from the activation of the non-rectifying NALCN which depolarized neurons and increased the likelihood of action potential generation independent of changes in VGSC function (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a finding from prior literature being discussed, supported by a citation.

claim: The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), was hypothesized to detect and transduce the [Ca2+]o changes and signal to the downstream multistep pathway.
source: The calcium-sensing receptor (CaSR), a G-protein-coupled receptor (GPCR), was hypothesized to detect and transduce the [Ca2+]o changes and signal to the downstream multistep pathway (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is a hypothesis from prior literature being discussed, supported by a citation.

claim: CaSR is well-positioned as a candidate [Ca2+]o detector because at nerve terminals it detects [Ca2+]o and regulates a non-selective cation channel.
source: CaSR is well-positioned as a candidate [Ca2+]o detector because at nerve terminals it detects [Ca2+]o and regulates a non-selective cation channel (Smith et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2010) and because it transduces changes in [Ca2+]o into NALCN activity following heterologous co-expression of CaSR, NALCN, UNC79, and UNC80 (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CaSR transduces changes in [Ca2+]o into NALCN activity following heterologous co-expression of CaSR, NALCN, UNC79, and UNC80.
source: CaSR is well-positioned as a candidate [Ca2+]o detector because at nerve terminals it detects [Ca2+]o and regulates a non-selective cation channel (Smith et al., 2004; Chen et al., 2010) and because it transduces changes in [Ca2+]o into NALCN activity following heterologous co-expression of CaSR, NALCN, UNC79, and UNC80 (Lu et al., 2010).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

claim: The UNC79-UNC80-NALCN pathway has an essential role in the maintenance of respiration.
source: Interest in the UNC79-UNC80-NALCN pathway has also risen, due to its essential role in the maintenance of respiration (Lu et al., 2007), the regulation of circadian rhythms (Lear et al., 2013; Flourakis et al., 2015), and because mutations of UNC80 and NALCN cause neurodevelopmental disorders, characterized by development delay and hypotonia (Al-Sayed et al., 2013; Perez et al., 2016).
evidence: This is supported by a citation to prior literature.

source: Switching from T1.1 to T0.2 shifted V0.5 by −11 mV and −9 mV in NesCre and Casr-/- neurons respectively (−46 ± 2 to −57 ± 2 mV and −43 ± 1 to −52 ± 1 mV).

claim: CaSR deletion shifted V0.5 for VGSC activation in a depolarizing direction (F (1, 17)=4.8, p=0.04).

claim: Divalent reduction hyperpolarized the region of overlap between VGSC inactivation and activation conductance plots toward the RMP, increasing the likelihood that persistent VGSC currents were activated at resting membrane potential.
source: Divalent reduction hyperpolarized this region of overlap toward the RMP (Figure 3F,G insets) increasing the likelihood that persistent VGSC currents were activated at resting membrane potential and therefore contributing to divalent-dependent excitability.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3F,G.

claim: The depolarization of VGSC activation gating that resulted from CaSR deletion shifted the area of conductance curve overlap for T0.2 in a depolarizing direction.
source: The depolarization of VGSC activation gating that resulted from CaSR deletion (Figure 3I), shifted the area of conductance curve overlap for T0.2 in a depolarizing direction (Figure 3G).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 3G,I.

claim: The shift in conductance curve overlap would reduce the fraction of VGSCs available for activation by T0.2 at the more hyperpolarized RMPs and explain the reduced the likelihood of spontaneous action potential generation in Casr-/- neurons.
source: This effect would reduce the fraction of VGSCs available for activation by T0.2 at the more hyperpolarized RMPs and explain the reduced the likelihood of spontaneous action potential generation in Casr-/- neurons (Figure 1).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: Neither the peak nor end VGPC current were affected by reduction of the external divalent concentration or by deletion of CaSR over the range of voltages tested.
source: Neither the peak nor end current were affected by reduction of the external divalent concentration or by deletion of CaSR (Figure 4) over the range of voltages.

claim: VGPC currents activated at 60 mV were unaffected by divalent concentration or CaSR deletion (F (3, 57)=1.347, p=0.2683 and (1, 19)=1.231, p=0.2811).

evidence: This is a statistical analysis result reported in the text and shown in Figure 4.

claim: VGPCs are not involved in divalent-dependent excitability in neocortical neurons.
source: These data indicate that VGPCs are not involved in divalent-dependent excitability in neocortical neurons.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 4.

claim: The switch from T1.1 to T0.2 elicited a basal current of -31 ± 3 pA (n = 13) at -70 mV in conWT neurons.
source: Since NALCN is resistant to the VGSC blocker tetrodotoxin (TTX) (Lu et al., 2007; Swayne et al., 2009) but Gd3+ (10 µM) inhibits NALCN and VGSCs (Elinder and Arhem, 1994; Li and Baumgarten, 2001; Lu et al., 2009), we were able to pharmacologically separate the contributions of VGSCs and NALCN to the basal current following the switch from T1.1 to T0.2 (-31 ± 3 pA, n = 13; Figure 5A–C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: Addition of a saturating concentration of TTX (1 µM) in T0.2 inhibited a persistent inward current within a few seconds in all but one of the recordings, consistent with VGSCs contributing to the inward current elicited by T0.2.
source: Addition of a saturating concentration of TTX (1 µM) in T0.2 inhibited a persistent inward current within a few seconds in all but one of the recordings (Figure 5A–C), consistent with VGSCs contributing to the inward current elicited by T0.2.
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5A-C.

claim: The TTX-sensitive divalent-dependent current was greater than the Gd3+-sensitive (p=0.039) and remaining divalent-dependent currents (p=0.0009).
source: Multiple comparison testing indicated that the TTX-sensitive divalent-dependent current was greater than the Gd3+-sensitive (p=0.039) and remaining divalent-dependent currents (p=0.0009; Table 14).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result reported in the text.

claim: The reduced sensitivity of neurons to the reduction of [Ca2+]o in the presence of TTX confirms that VGSCs are the major contributor to the depolarizing current elicited by low [Ca2+]o.
source: While there were rare neurons in which there was a larger Gd3+-sensitive current (Figure 5C) the reduced sensitivity of neurons to the reduction of [Ca2+]o in the presence of TTX, confirms that VGSCs are the major contributor to the depolarizing current elicited by low [Ca2+]o.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: By interpolation, the contribution of NALCN and VGSCs to divalent-dependent currents were equal at −77 mV with the contribution from VGSCs increasing with depolarization.
source: By interpolation (Figure 5G, inset), the contribution of NALCN and VGSCs to divalent-dependent currents were equal at −77 mV with the contribution from VGSCs increasing with depolarization.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 5G.

claim: Divalent-dependent currents around the resting membrane that contribute to divalent-dependent excitability are mainly attributable to VGSCs.
source: These data indicate that divalent-dependent currents around the resting membrane that contribute to divalent-dependent excitability are mainly attributable to VGSCs.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 5.

claim: Switching from T1.1 to T0.2 depolarized the membrane potential from −70 mV by 7.2 ± 1.5 mV (n = 12) and increased spontaneous action potential firing in pharmacologically isolated conWT neurons.
source: Consistent with earlier experiments (Figure 2), switching from T1.1 to T0.2 depolarized the membrane potential from −70 mV by 7.2 ± 1.5 mV (n = 12) and increased spontaneous action potential firing in pharmacologically isolated neurons (Figure 6A,B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6A,B.

claim: TTX blocked action potential generation and also hyperpolarized the membrane potential indicating that VGSCs were open in T0.2 and T1.1.
source: TTX blocked action potential generation, as expected, but also hyperpolarized the membrane potential indicating that VGSCs were open in T0.2 (Figure 6A1) and T1.1 (Figure 6A2).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6A.

claim: On average the divalent-dependent depolarization was almost entirely prevented by TTX or TTX and Gd3+ co-application.
source: On average the divalent-dependent depolarization was almost entirely prevented by TTX or TTX and Gd3+ co-application (Figure 6B).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6B.

claim: The amplitude of the divalent-dependent depolarizations in conWT neurons changed with blocker type (1-way RM ANOVA, F (1.219, 13.41)=12.83, p=0.0022).
source: The amplitude of the divalent-dependent depolarizations in conWT neurons changed with blocker type (1-way RM ANOVA, F (1.219, 13.41)=12.83, p=0.0022, Table 15).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result reported in the text.

claim: The TTX-sensitive component of divalent-dependent depolarization was greater than the Gd3+-sensitive and the blocker-resistant component (p=0.022 and 0.0028 respectively).
source: The TTX-sensitive component was greater than the Gd3+-sensitive and the blocker-resistant component (p=0.022 and 0.0028 respectively, Table 16).
evidence: This is a statistical analysis result reported in the text.

claim: On average VGSCs accounted for 93% of the depolarization that triggers divalent-dependent excitability in WT neurons starting at −70 mV.
source: On average VGSCs accounted for 93% of the depolarization that triggers divalent-dependent excitability in WT neurons starting at −70 mV (Figure 6C) and we observed a similar pattern in Casr-/- neurons (Figure 6C).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 6C.

claim: VGSC currents were the major contributor to divalent-dependent currents over the −77 to −30 mV voltage range.
source: The VGSC currents were the major contributor to divalent-dependent currents over the −77 to −30 mV voltage range (Figure 6D,E).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations shown in Figure 6D,E.

claim: VGSCs are the predominant contributor to the depolarizations that lead to action potential generation at lower external divalent concentrations.
source: These findings indicate that VGSCs are the predominant contributor to the depolarizations that lead to action potential generation at lower external divalent concentrations (Figure 6E, gray bar).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The vast majority of divalent-dependent neuronal excitability was mediated via VGSCs in three ways.
source: We found no evidence that this specific mechanism was active in neocortical neurons (Figure 2). Instead, we determined that the vast majority of divalent-dependent neuronal excitability was mediated via VGSCs in three ways.
evidence: This is a major conclusion of the study, summarizing the findings.

claim: Decreasing the concentration of external divalents activated VGSCs at the resting membrane potential and depolarized the membrane toward the action potential threshold.
source: Decreasing the concentration of external divalents activated VGSCs at the resting membrane potential and depolarized the membrane toward the action potential threshold (Figure 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 6.

claim: The decreased divalent concentration hyperpolarized the VGSC window current toward the membrane potential increasing sodium currents and the likelihood of action potential generation.
source: This occurred because the decreased divalent concentration hyperpolarized the VGSC window current toward the membrane potential increasing sodium currents and the likelihood of action potential generation (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a mechanistic explanation supported by experimental data in Figure 3.

claim: Deletion of CaSR modulated VGSC gating, decreasing the sensitivity of current activation to depolarization via an unidentified mechanism.
source: Unexpectedly the deletion of CaSR modulated VGSC gating, decreasing the sensitivity of current activation to depolarization via an unidentified mechanism (Figure 3).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 3.

claim: Deletion of CaSR also indirectly affected action potential generation by modestly hyperpolarizing the membrane potential.
source: Deletion of CaSR also indirectly affected action potential generation by modestly hyperpolarizing the membrane potential (Figure 1).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figure 1.

claim: Using Gd3+ we isolated small divalent-dependent inward currents in about half of the neurons.
source: While the actions of [Ca2+]o on VGSCs were responsible for the vast majority of the [Ca2+]o-dependent neuronal excitability, using Gd3+ we isolated small divalent-dependent inward currents in about half of the neurons (Figure 5).
evidence: This is a direct experimental observation reported in the text and shown in Figure 5.

claim: The Gd3+-sensitive currents presumably reflected activation of NALCN, and were unaffected by CaSR deletion.
source: These Gd3+-sensitive currents presumably reflected activation of NALCN, and were unaffected by CaSR deletion, but their relatively small size compared to TTX-sensitive divalent-dependent inward currents indicate that they would be minor contributors to divalent-dependent excitability compared to VGSCs (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations.

claim: The Gd3+-sensitive currents were relatively small compared to TTX-sensitive divalent-dependent inward currents indicating they would be minor contributors to divalent-dependent excitability compared to VGSCs.
source: These Gd3+-sensitive currents presumably reflected activation of NALCN, and were unaffected by CaSR deletion, but their relatively small size compared to TTX-sensitive divalent-dependent inward currents indicate that they would be minor contributors to divalent-dependent excitability compared to VGSCs (Figures 5 and 6).
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 5 and 6.

claim: The fractions of the divalent-dependent currents and depolarizations that were sensitive to TTX were surprisingly large compared to those that were Gd3+-sensitive indicating the relative importance of VGSC- and NALCN-mediated contributions to divalent-dependent excitability respectively.
source: The fractions of the divalent-dependent currents and depolarizations that were sensitive to TTX were surprisingly large compared to those that were Gd3+-sensitive (Figures 5D and 6C) indicating the relative importance of VGSC- and NALCN-mediated contributions to divalent-dependent excitability respectively.
evidence: This is a conclusion drawn from the experimental data presented in Figures 5D and 6C.

claim: Persistent subthreshold VGSC currents have been shown to determine spiking rates in other central neurons.
source: Persistent subthreshold VGSC currents have been shown to determine spiking rates in other central neurons (Taddese and Bean, 2002; Gorelova and Seamans, 2015) and so the increased VGSC currents we observed in T0.2 are well-positioned to explain the increased action potential frequency (Figure 6).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The increased VGSC currents observed in T0.2 are well-positioned to explain the increased action potential frequency.
source: Persistent subthreshold VGSC currents have been shown to determine spiking rates in other central neurons (Taddese and Bean, 2002; Gorelova and Seamans, 2015) and so the increased VGSC currents we observed in T0.2 are well-positioned to explain the increased action potential frequency (Figure 6).
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental observations and prior literature.

claim: The physiological impact of VGSC-mediated divalent-dependent excitability may be enormous overall because of the dynamic nature of [Ca2+]o in vivo where it decreases from basal (1.1–1.2 mM) by 30–80%.
source: However, the physiological impact of VGSC-mediated divalent-dependent excitability may be enormous overall because of the dynamic nature of [Ca2+]oin vivo where it decreases from basal (1.1–1.2 mM) by 30–80% (Nicholson et al., 1978; Ohta et al., 1997; Pietrobon and Moskowitz, 2014).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: The overall computational effects of physiological decrements in [Ca2+]o will be complex because the increased action potential generation due to changes on VGSCs will be confounded by the impact of reduced Ca2+ entry through VACCs, reduced excitatory synaptic transmission, and altered CaSR-mediated signaling at the nerve terminal.
source: The overall computational effects of physiological decrements in [Ca2+]o will be complex because the increased action potential generation due to changes on VGSCs (Figures 3 and 6) will be confounded by the impact of reduced Ca2+ entry through VACCs (Hess et al., 1986; Weber et al., 2010; Williams et al., 2012), reduced excitatory synaptic transmission (Neher and Sakaba, 2008; Vyleta and Smith, 2011), and altered CaSR-mediated signaling at the nerve terminal (Phillips et al., 2008; Chen et al., 2010; Vyleta and Smith, 2011).
evidence: This is a speculative statement supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: CaSR and surface charge screening are both sensitive to Ca2+ and Mg2+ with Ca2+ being two to three times more effective in both processes.
source: CaSR and sodium conductance gating are both sensitive to Ca2+ and Mg2+, with Ca2+ being two to three times more potent in both processes (Frankenhaeuser and Hodgkin, 1957; Brown et al., 1993).
evidence: This is supported by citations to prior literature.

claim: Divalent-dependent excitability in neurons is largely attributable to actions of extracellular calcium on the VGSC function.
source: Overall, our studies indicate that divalent-dependent excitability in neurons is largely attributable to actions of extracellular calcium on the VGSC function.
evidence: This is the main conclusion of the study, supported by multiple experimental findings throughout the manuscript.

claim: Given the dynamic nature of brain extracellular calcium, the VGSC mechanism is likely to impact neuronal signaling greatly under physiological and pathological conditions.
source: Given the dynamic nature of brain extracellular calcium, this mechanism is likely to impact neuronal signaling greatly under physiological and pathological conditions.
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings and general knowledge.

claim: CaSR-dependent reduction of VGSC sensitivity to membrane potential adds further complexity to extracellular calcium signaling and identifies another potential mechanism by which CaSR stimulation may influence neuronal death following stroke and traumatic brain injury.
source: CaSR-dependent reduction of VGSC sensitivity to membrane potential adds further complexity to extracellular calcium signaling and identifies another potential mechanism by which CaSR stimulation may influence neuronal death following stroke and traumatic brain injury (Kim et al., 2013; Hannan et al., 2018).
evidence: This is a speculative conclusion based on the study findings and supported by citations to prior literature.
